extracted.intended_audience: students, instructors, and researchers in media studies and journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating patterns, biases, and influences in mass media content (news, television, magazines) using demographic, power, and institutional benchmarks. Includes attention to representation (gender, race, age, class, sexual orientation), source selection, and hierarchical influences on content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latino undercoverage and negative stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: Brutality is generally presented as a 'black-white' problem, ignoring 'the many Latino uprisings related to police abuses' and 'Few Latinos are covered at all, and they become victims of negative stereotypes' (Jordan, 1992).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Coverage often omits Latino incidents and frames Latinos through negative stereotypes. Use demographic comparisons to reveal such omission and examine framing language that casts Latinos as victims or deviants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minority marking vs. white/default invisibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If the subject of a news story is a white male, there is rarely any reference to his gender or race, but 'black leader' and 'female candidate' are all too typical of references to minorities and women in the news (Gersh, October 1992).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: look for asymmetry in labels — whether race/gender is marked for minorities but not for white males; such marking signals 'othering' and unequal treatment in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical underrepresentation of women
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Despite the hype about 1992 being the `Year of the Woman,' for the fifth year in a row women were found to be significantly underrepresented in American newspapers and on network news programs' (Gersh, 1993).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure proportion of women featured vs population benchmarks and track trends over time; note differences across media types (e.g., news magazines vs television news).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypical roles and occupational portrayals of women
rubrics_metrics.description: Women are outnumbered, young, and overrepresented in lower level jobs, situation comedies, and family dramas; when depicted with men they are most often shown in inferior capacities (e.g., male doctor with female nurse) and commercials often neglect or stereotype women in domestic roles (Greenberg, 1980; Signorielli, 1985).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess role types, job prestige, relational positioning (dependent/inferior), and commercial portrayals (voice-over assignments). Look for persistence of domestic and sexualized tropes in programming and advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age representation bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Older men are more apt to be seen on television than older women, directly contrary to the ratio in real life; both very young and very old are underrepresented and negatively stereotyped (Greenberg, 1980; Signorielli, 1985).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare age distribution of on-screen characters with census/population data; examine differences by gender (older men treated more favorably than older women).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gendered depiction of violence and victimization
rubrics_metrics.description: Males in television series commit antisocial acts and are involved in physically aggressive acts more often than females; females are more likely than males to be depicted as victims, with women in minority roles more likely to suffer violence than to inflict it (Greenberg, 1980; Gerbner et al., 1982; Signorielli, 1985).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code perpetrators vs victims by gender and intersectional status (age, race, class). Interpreted as a shorthand for power—who can victimize and who is powerless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection of gender and social class in portrayals
rubrics_metrics.description: An inverted relationship between social class and gender exists in situation comedies: for working-class families fathers are shown as weak and mothers competent; for middle-class families fathers easily meet competency standards (Butsch, 1992).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate portrayals across class contexts to detect gender-status inversions and variations in competence depictions tied to class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women's magazine fiction stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: In women's magazines fictional women were defined by the absence or presence of men, work for women was treated as secondary to home life, heroines tended to be young and attractive, few were low socioeconomic status or nondominant ethnic groups (Franzwa, 1974; Wilson, 1981).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze magazine fiction for dependency narratives, occupational status, age/attractiveness norms, and ethnic/class diversity among protagonists.

rubrics_metrics.name: News coverage bias toward women's minority/novelty status rather than issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Most coverage of women in the 1970s dealt with their entry into the professions and politics—making them newsworthy because of their minority characteristic. Coverage of women politicians received less attention to issue stands and more to viability as candidates (Kahn & Goldenberg, 1991).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether stories frame women as 'newsworthy' because they are atypical and whether coverage emphasizes personality/viability over policy positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective framing of public-health and social problems (AIDS example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although women are 10 times as likely as men to contract HIV through heterosexual sex, media coverage centers on female prostitutes and the chance they may spread the disease, with little coverage on how prostitutes become HIV infected (Devitt, 1993).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine causal framing and focus—whether media explore structural causes and contexts or instead frame marginalized groups as vectors of risk without contextual explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmarking media content against demographic/geographic standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Some content studies explicitly compare media patterns with demographic, geographic, and other external benchmarks to see whether media worlds differ in predictable ways (e.g., representation proportional to population, land mass, ethnic distribution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological criterion: use external benchmarks (population, geography, historical trends) for calibration, but recognize limits—news and drama purposively select non-proportional slices of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: News selection based on impact and deviation from proportionality
rubrics_metrics.description: News is more efficient when it alerts us to things that have an impact on our lives; thus some selection away from proportional representation is inherent because news emphasizes events with consequence rather than simply mirroring population slices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating proportionality, account for the functional logic of news (impact, timeliness, deviance). Distinguish legitimate news selection from systematic exclusion tied to power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power relations as a central explanatory criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: If each person were equally powerful, media attention might be spread according to population; because power is uneven, media reflect power relations—who is seen most frequently matters and indicates who matters most (Parenti, 1978; Gerbner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use power indicators (wealth, political access, institutional position) to explain patterns of coverage and representation; assess whether media attention correlates with measures of social power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic annihilation/minimization of less powerful groups
rubrics_metrics.description: The media have the ability to express lack of power by minimizing people through 'symbolic annihilation,' by under- or misrepresenting them (Tuchman, 1981).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for absence, trivialization, or stereotyped depictions as signs of symbolic annihilation; quantify omissions and misrepresentations relative to societal presence and significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geography-of-power criterion in coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Which states or countries are mentioned most often? Those on the East and West Coasts and powerful countries internationally—media attention follows geographic concentrations of financial, political, and cultural power (e.g., New York, Washington, Los Angeles; Western world and former communist-bloc).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map coverage frequency geographically and compare to centers of political/economic/cultural influence; evaluate overseas coverage for imbalance favoring powerful nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source selection bias toward officials and elites
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations rely on officials and other wealthy, corporate, and bureaucratic elites as routine sources; less powerful people or causes gain attention mainly when they become extremists and are often evaluated through establishment sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code sources in stories (officials, corporate, grassroots) and assess diversity; critique reliance on elite sources as a bias that narrows viewpoints and frames outsiders via establishment lenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviance framing differences for powerful vs powerless
rubrics_metrics.description: When the powerful commit deviant acts (e.g., white-collar crime), those violations receive less attention than crimes by the powerless; less powerful people are taken seriously mainly as threats to the status quo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare attention, framing, and investigative depth allocated to misconduct by elites versus non-elites; evaluate whether systemic harms by the powerful are undercovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media consonance and agenda-setting power
rubrics_metrics.description: There is commonality among content presented by various media ('media consonance'); when media converge around a few key sources and interpretations, fewer 'voices' remain and the media have more power to influence audiences—the most powerful media help to 'set the agenda' and define reality for less powerful media (Reese, 1991).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cross-media convergence of frames and sources; evaluate concentration of agenda-setting influence and the resultant narrowing of public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media as cultural magnifier and feedback mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Media content takes elements of culture, magnifies them, frames them, and feeds them back to an audience—media impose their own logic; content may serve as either a catalyst for or a brake on social change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing media effects, consider how repeated portrayals amplify social norms and either reinforce or inhibit social change; analyze cyclical feedback between media representation and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchical model of influences on content
rubrics_metrics.description: Influences on content operate at multiple levels: individual (communicator characteristics, attitudes, roles), routines, organizational constraints, extramedia factors (economic environment, advertisers, culture), and ideology of the powerful (hegemony); higher-level influences (extramedia, ideology) have broader societal impact than routine-level influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the hierarchy to attribute observed content patterns to appropriate causes; prioritize analysis of extramedia and ideological influences when seeking explanations for systematic, societally consequential patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicators' characteristics and professional backgrounds as influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics intrinsic to communicators—gender, ethnicity, sexual orientation, education, professional background, years of experience—influence content indirectly via attitudes and directly via professional roles and ethics. Example: the 'typical' U.S. journalist described as a white Protestant male with specific career attributes (Weaver & Wilhoit, 1992).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate newsroom composition and career-stage demographics to understand potential biases; consider retention and promotion patterns (e.g., minority and women representation at different experience levels) when diagnosing content outcomes.
